blocks.text: Matthew closes with the empty tomb, appearances of the risen Jesus, and a meeting in Galilee where the eleven receive their final commission. The chapter also includes a competing explanation of the empty tomb: the guards are instructed to say that the disciples stole the body. This makes the chapter attend both to its resurrection proclamation and to a counterclaim about it.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary are not merely present at the tomb. In Matthew’s narrative, they witness Jesus’ death and burial, find the tomb empty, receive the angel’s message, meet the risen Jesus, and are sent to tell his brothers. Their role carries the resurrection news from the tomb to the disciples.

At the Galilean mountain, the disciples worship Jesus, yet the text says that some—or possibly the group as a whole—also hesitate or doubt. The wording leaves the precise subject open, preserving a scene in which worship and uncertainty stand together.

Jesus’ commission is not simply an instruction to gain adherents. It describes making disciples among all nations through baptism and teaching people to observe what Jesus commanded. The authority claimed in verse 18 frames that charge, while the promise of continuing presence closes it. The commission cannot ethically be used to authorize coercive conversion, forced baptism, colonial domination, cultural erasure, or religious violence.

The final command reaches “all nations,” in contrast with Matthew’s earlier presentation of a mission focused on Israel. Verse 19 also gives baptism its threefold wording: “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” a form supported by the extant Greek manuscript tradition and later central to Trinitarian reception.
